To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the neural mass model reproduces exactly the dynamics of a heterogeneous network composed of many excitatoy populations and a common inhibition.

a population model of neural mass dynamics can reproduce exactly the dynamics and the oscillatory activity of spiking networks and that it is able to reproduce several experimental results on human and non human primate WM.
the WM capacity of the model is comparable to the one measured in humans.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of a population model able to capture several aspects of WM, including the capacity and the memory load, in agreement with experimental observations.
the development and the validation of a new theoretical approach to study the dynamics of WM in the cortex.
the development of a novel theoretical framework able to reproduce the dynamics of spikes neural networks with synaptic plasticity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our population model reproduces exactly the dynamics of large scale neural networks and that it is able to capture several WM operations and related experimental data.
we have developed an innovative neural mass model able, for the first time, to reproduce the dynamics of heterogeneous neural networks with realistic synapses and cellular mechanisms.

the model is able to reproduce the dynamics of spiny stellate neurons in layer 4 of the primary somatosensory cortex during vibrotacile stimuli in humans, and of pyramidal neurons in the prefrontal cortex during object recognition in monkeys, as well as the dynamics of a spiking neural network composed of hundreds of thousand neurons with realistic synaptic plasticities during WM tasks in humans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our model provides a new theoretical framework to investigate the neural basis of WM and to test the validity of our model against experimental data.
we have provided the theoretical foundations of the synaptic theory of working memory.
we have developed a novel model able to reproduce several WM operations and to provide new tools to measure WM capacity in humans and animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a simple neural mass model with realistic synaptic mechanisms is able to mimic the brain dynamics during WM operations.
WM is a dynamical process that can be efficiently modeled in a coarse grained way, without the need of a large number of microscopic neurons.
synaptic plasticity is a suitable mechanism to sustain memory storage and operations.
